definition: A biohybrid microswimmer also known as biohybrid nanorobot, can be defined as a microswimmer that consist of both biological and artificial constituents, for instance, one or several living microorganisms attached to one or various synthetic parts.
details: In recent years nanoscopic and mesoscopic objects have been designed to collectively move through direct inspiration from nature or by harnessing its existing tools. Small mesoscopic to nanoscopic systems typically operate at low Reynolds numbers (Re ≪ 1), and understanding their motion becomes challenging. For locomotion to occur, the symmetry of the system must be broken. In addition, collective motion requires a coupling mechanism between the entities that make up the collective. To develop mesoscopic to nanoscopic entities capable of swarming behaviour, it has been hypothesised that the entities are characterised by broken symmetry with a well-defined morphology, and are powered with some material capable of harvesting energy. If the harvested energy results in a field surrounding the object, then this field can couple with the field of a neighbouring object and bring some coordination to the collective behaviour. Such robotic swarms have been categorised by an online expert panel as among the 10 great unresolved group challenges in the area of robotics. explainer.lead: A biohybrid microswimmer combines a living microorganism with synthetic parts to make a tiny object that can swim. Researchers study these systems to understand motion at very small scales and how many such objects might coordinate as a swarm.

tiers.eli5: Imagine giving a tiny living swimmer a small artificial backpack, so the living part and the made part move as one. At this scale, water feels very different from the water we swim in, and the swimmer needs an uneven shape to get anywhere. Scientists also want many of these swimmers to move together.
tiers.practitioner: A biohybrid design pairs one or more living microorganisms with synthetic components and treats the assembly as a low-Reynolds-number swimmer. The design must break symmetry for locomotion, harvest energy through a suitable material, and, for collective motion, provide a coupling mechanism between neighbouring entities. The mechanisms underlying these systems remain at an early stage of investigation.
tiers.paperLevel: A biohybrid microswimmer is a microswimmer composed of biological and artificial constituents, typically one or several living microorganisms attached to synthetic parts. These systems operate at Re << 1, where locomotion requires broken symmetry; proposed swarming behaviour additionally requires energy harvesting and field-mediated coupling between neighbouring objects. Their mechanisms of action and collective coordination remain unresolved research challenges.

explainer.example: A living microorganism attached to a synthetic body forms one biohybrid microswimmer. If its asymmetric shape lets it swim and its energy-harvesting material creates a field, that field can couple with a neighbouring swimmer's field and help coordinate the pair.

explainer.intuition: The living microorganism supplies a biological component, while attached synthetic parts complete a tiny swimming machine. Making one swimmer move is only the first challenge; getting many to coordinate requires their behaviour to influence one another.
howItWorks: Attach one or several living microorganisms to one or more synthetic parts.
Give the combined entity broken symmetry and a well-defined morphology so locomotion can occur at low Reynolds number.
Use a material capable of harvesting energy to power the entity.
If harvesting produces a surrounding field, let that field interact with a neighbour's field.
Use these interactions to coordinate aspects of the collective's motion.
explainer.whyItMatters: Biohybrid microswimmers connect the design of individual microscopic swimmers with the harder problem of coordinated swarm behaviour. Such robotic swarms have been categorised by an online expert panel as one of robotics' ten great unresolved group challenges.
misconceptions: It is not entirely artificial: living biological constituents are part of the swimmer.
An asymmetric swimmer is not automatically a coordinated swarm; collective motion also needs coupling between entities.
